content: The proportion of individuals diagnosed with chronic hepatitis C (HCV viremic infection) is calculated from the estimated population with hepatitis C. Among those diagnosed, the proportion assessed for treatment eligibility is determined using non-invasive tests for liver staging, such as the APRI score and ALT levels. Finally, the proportion of individuals achieving sustained viral response at week 12 after initiating treatment is also tracked. At the early stages of a program, the care cascade may be estimated using ad hoc methods, such as surveys, data from treatment cohorts in tertiary hospitals, and medicine sales records. However, the most effective way to monitor a national hepatitis B and C testing and treatment program is by establishing a patient-centered data monitoring system. This system should be integrated into the broader governance framework of the national health management information system, as outlined in Chapter 6 on person-centered patient monitoring. At global, regional, or national levels, care cascades are ideally presented in relation to the infected population. Modeled care cascades can be used to track progress at regional and global levels. At subnational levels, where the denominator of those with chronic infection may not be available or where estimating the catchment area of healthcare facilities is challenging, the cascade is presented using service delivery data. Various platforms are used to report care cascades and program coverage targets. Program officers are encouraged to use this guidance for national monitoring and reporting and to utilize the resulting data for WHO global reporting or validating hepatitis elimination efforts. Reporting should include detailed methods for calculating care cascade data, which should be documented in government reports and websites. The Monitoring and Evaluation Framework for Viral Hepatitis B and C includes specific indicators for program reporting. For example, the proportion of individuals diagnosed with chronic hepatitis B or C, those initiating antiviral therapy, and those achieving viral suppression or cure are key metrics. Treatment eligibility criteria vary across countries and should align with the latest WHO guidelines or regional/national standards. Person-centered data is essential for organizing health services around the needs and expectations of individuals and communities. Such data supports longitudinal monitoring of patients, improves the quality and continuity of care, and enhances data collection, recording, and reporting through investments in digital health systems like electronic medical records. These systems also facilitate the aggregation of data for surveillance and program monitoring, reducing errors and delays while easing the reporting burden on healthcare workers. Person-centered data systems are critical for tracking the health status of individuals with chronic viral hepatitis over time, monitoring program performance, and allocating resources efficiently. These systems must capture data on both acute and chronic infections, as well as long-term sequelae like liver cirrhosis and cancer. Integration and triangulation of data from different parts of the health system are necessary for comprehensive analysis. Healthcare providers can use person-centered data to improve services, such as following up with patients who miss appointments or understanding factors affecting access to prevention and treatment services. For example, data on hepatitis B birth-dose vaccine coverage, screening of pregnant women, and antiviral prophylaxis for eligible individuals are crucial for eliminating mother-to-child transmission of hepatitis B. Testing data should be collected and analyzed to understand testing patterns, retesting, and results, particularly for high-risk populations like people who inject drugs. Standardized data approaches across various testing settings are needed to improve care and service delivery. Linkage to treatment and care is essential for achieving programmatic impact. Monitoring systems should enable longitudinal tracking of patients, including viral load suppression for hepatitis B and cure confirmation for hepatitis C. Patient monitoring for chronic viral hepatitis should be integrated with systems for other associated conditions, such as HIV, sexually transmitted infections, and tuberculosis. Over time, countries should aim to integrate hepatitis monitoring systems with those for other chronic conditions like diabetes and liver disease. Linking databases for monitoring hepatitis sequelae, such as liver cancer registries, is also important. Data confidentiality and security are critical when using health data, especially given the risks of stigma, discrimination, or legal consequences. Countries should invest in secure data systems with clear governance policies to protect patient privacy. WHO encourages the sharing of person-centered data for public health purposes, provided it is done with patient consent and safeguards against misuse. A minimum data set for monitoring hepatitis includes standardized demographic, clinical, and laboratory data elements. This data set captures key interactions along the care cascade and supports reporting on core indicators. Countries are encouraged to embed hepatitis surveillance within national health sector planning processes. A stepwise approach is recommended for establishing data systems, starting with surveys to estimate epidemiology and natural history, followed by routine program data for managing and monitoring testing and treatment coverage. Person-centered data systems are essential for scaling up hepatitis programs and achieving elimination goals.
